name: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) — county-level unemployment rate and labor force
gap: No employment/labor-market signal exists anywhere in this codebase today (grep for unemployment/LAUS/employment turned up nothing). Local job-market strength is a classic housing-demand driver an investor would care about, and it's missing entirely from the Growth Score inputs.
granularity: county (and MSA, city) monthly estimates for ~7,600 areas
license: BLS is a federal statistical agency; its published data is standard US-government public-domain data. Not independently re-confirmed this run (bls.gov wasn't fetched directly — see network note below), but this is the normal, low-risk case (same category as Census, which this project already treats as clean).
cost: Free. BLS's Public Data API is usable without registration at low volume; v2 (needed for the request volume a monthly multi-county pull would use) needs a free registration key, same pattern as Census/FRED. A bulk flat-file alternative also exists (ZIP download of county labor-force data) for the last ~14 months without any key, with longer history via BLS's own database query tool.
history: Monthly county data available back to roughly 1990 via the query tools; exact start varies by series/area.
proposed_kind: neighborhood — would map county -> NYC's 5 boroughs -> NTA.
correlation: not computed — app/research/evaluate_series.py does not exist yet.
recommendation_detail: Rank #3, don't implement yet. For NYC specifically, LAUS is county-level and NYC's 5 counties are exactly the 5 boroughs — so this would give only 5 distinct values spread across this project's ~200 NTAs (neighborhoods within the same borough would all score identically on this metric). Per backend/CLAUDE.md's scoring invariant, every metric becomes a percentile within its comparison set, and a 5-value metric percentiled across 200 neighborhoods carries very little information at NYC's current granularity. This gets much more useful once the area-model migration moves comparison sets to CBSA (county-level data is a natural fit for comparing *across* metros, where county is often the right granularity). Recommend revisiting after that migration rather than implementing now.
